lesson.title: The One-Way Fingerprint: What Hash Functions Actually Guarantee
lesson.summary: A cryptographic hash function takes any input and produces a fixed size fingerprint that is practically impossible to reverse or fake a collision for, which makes it a tool for verifying integrity, not a form of encryption.
lesson.body:
A cryptographic hash function takes an input of any length, a single word, a short message, or an entire multi gigabyte file, and produces an output of a fixed size, called a digest or hash. SHA-256, one of the most widely used hash functions today, always produces a 256 bit output no matter what you feed it. Feed it three bytes or three gigabytes, and you still get back exactly 256 bits.

A cryptographic hash function needs to satisfy a few properties to be useful. It must be one way, meaning that given a digest, there is no practical way to work backward and recover the original input, a property called preimage resistance. It must be deterministic, so the same input always produces the same output, which is what makes it useful for verification at all. It must exhibit an avalanche effect, meaning that changing even a single character of the input produces a wildly different, unrecognizable output, so that similar inputs never produce similar looking digests. And it must be collision resistant, meaning that although, strictly by the pigeonhole principle, there are infinitely many possible inputs mapping to a finite set of fixed size outputs so collisions must mathematically exist somewhere, finding two different inputs that produce the same digest must be computationally infeasible in practice.

The avalanche effect is easy to see directly. Computing the real SHA-256 digest of the five letter word hello gives 2cf24dba5fb0a30e26e83b2ac5b9e29e1b161e5c1fa7425e73043362938b9824. Capitalizing just the first letter, so the input becomes Hello, gives 185f8db32271fe25f561a6fc938b2e264306ec304eda518007d1764826381969. One character changed, and the two 64 character hexadecimal digests share essentially no resemblance to each other. There is no way to look at those two digests and guess that the inputs were nearly identical, and that is precisely the point: a hash reveals nothing about how close two inputs are.

It is worth being explicit about something that trips people up: a hash function is not encryption. Symmetric encryption, from a few chapters back, is deliberately reversible, that is the entire purpose of the key, to turn ciphertext back into plaintext. A hash function has no key and is deliberately not reversible at all. You cannot unhash a digest to recover the original message, because a hash function is not designed to preserve the information needed to do that, it is designed to destroy it while still producing a consistent fingerprint.

That one way property is exactly what makes hashing useful. A file's publisher can post the hash of a file alongside the download, and anyone who downloads it can hash their own copy and compare, catching corruption or tampering without needing to compare the entire file byte for byte. Systems that need to check a password without storing it in readable form can store only its hash, so that even someone who steals the stored data does not get back the original password, only its fingerprint. And, as the next chapter builds on directly, hashing turns out to be one of the two essential ingredients, alongside public key cryptography, in how digital signatures actually work.
